idiom_name: not applicable - policy objects (Strategy) with generics only for types
implementation_notes: Policy-based design does not survive Java's type erasure: a generic class is shared by all its invocations, type parameters do not exist at run time, cannot be instantiated, and cannot drive static dispatch, and the language has no template-template equivalent - Oracle's own generics guide states that generics 'do not generate a new class for each specialization, nor do they permit template metaprogramming'. The substitutable axis is therefore an injected strategy object or functional interface (Comparator<T>, Function<T,R>, UnaryOperator<T>), chosen at construction time; bounded type parameters (T extends Comparable<T>) constrain the types a host accepts, not the behaviour it runs, and must not be presented as policies. Prefer the injected form when the variant is a runtime or configuration decision, and plain subclasses when the variation is genuinely closed.
alternative: Strategy - an interface-typed field or functional interface (Comparator, Function, UnaryOperator) injected through the constructor or a DI container; because Java erases type parameters, a type argument cannot carry behaviour into the host, so the runtime form is the only honest realization (lambda-based strategies cover the single-method axes).
pitfalls: Bounded type parameters look like policies but only restrict the accepted types; expecting compile-time behaviour selection leads to reflection, unchecked casts and bridge-method surprises.
Erased generics make it illegal to instantiate a type parameter or declare static fields typed by it, so a policy can never be default-constructed from the type argument.
Injected policies are shared by reference: a mutable strategy object used by many hosts changes all of them, and lambdas capturing state silently close over the creating scope.
